passage:
Dear Professor Usha,
Thank you for your comments on my thesis proposal. I understand you think the second topic, on water pricing in small towns, has better data and a clearer method. I agree it's probably stronger on paper. But I'd really like to continue with my first draft on street-vendor apps. I've spent a lot of time on it, and honestly it feels like mine in a way the new topic doesn't. I know you said the data is thin, and that two seniors dropped similar ideas. Still, I think if I work harder, the draft can get there. Could we meet on Thursday so I can explain why it's worth more than it looks?
Regards,
Vishal

qa.q: What is the second topic, which Professor Usha preferred, about?
qa.a: The second topic is about water pricing in small towns.

qa.q: Why does Vishal want to keep the first draft after agreeing the second topic is stronger?
qa.a: Vishal feels attached and protective toward the first draft because, after so much time spent on it, it feels like Vishal's own. So it seems worth more than it is, even with thin data.

qa.q: What question could Vishal ask before Thursday's meeting?
qa.a: Vishal could ask: if both topics were brand new today, which would I pick? That strips away the extra value the draft gets just from being mine.

qa.q: How might Professor Usha read this email?
qa.a: The professor may notice that the only reason given is that the draft feels like Vishal's, and prepare to gently compare both topics on data and method.

grounding: Shows a student refusing to drop a first draft because it feels like the student's own, valuing it above a better alternative.

passage: Avni, before you say anything, yes, I know the scooter is old. I'm Kashish, and that red scooter has carried me through three years of college. The mechanic says it's worth maybe eighteen thousand. Eighteen! I told the buyer who came yesterday I won't take less than forty. He laughed and left. Everyone keeps saying a new electric one would save me money every month and I'd stop pushing this one up the hostel slope. But this one knows me. The dent on the side is from my first fall. Would I pay forty thousand for someone else's old scooter with a dent? Obviously not. That's different, though. This one is mine.

qa.q: What is the scooter worth, according to the mechanic?
qa.a: The mechanic says it's worth maybe eighteen thousand.

qa.q: Why does Kashish ask forty thousand when the mechanic says eighteen?
qa.a: Kashish feels fond of and protective about the scooter because it holds three years of memories, like the dent from the first fall. So it seems worth far more than the market says.

qa.q: What could Kashish do with the question already asked out loud?
qa.a: Kashish could take "would I pay forty for someone else's?" seriously and price the scooter as a buyer would, keeping the memories in photos rather than in a high price.

qa.q: How might the buyer who laughed see Kashish's price?
qa.a: The buyer likely saw forty thousand as unrealistic for an old dented scooter and felt there was no point in bargaining.

grounding: Shows a student refusing to sell an old scooter at market value because of owning it, pricing it far above what buyers pay.

passage: I'm Simran, and I'm in Tarun's design studio group. For our final project, he made the first concept for the bus shelter: a curved roof like a leaf. Everyone liked it at first. Then Rekha ma'am showed us a second concept from another member: simpler, cheaper, and better at keeping rain out. Even Tarun admitted the leaf roof leaked in the model. But he wouldn't let it go. "I've built three models of this," he said. "It's mine. It's more original." He spent the whole weekend fixing leaks instead of helping with the new one. I don't know if he really thinks it's better or just can't give it up.

qa.q: What shape was Tarun's first concept roof?
qa.a: It was a curved roof like a leaf.

qa.q: Why does Tarun keep fixing the leaf roof after admitting it leaks?
qa.a: Tarun feels attached and protective of the leaf roof because he built three models and it is his idea. So it feels more valuable to him than the simpler design, even though the other one works better.

qa.q: What could the group suggest to help Tarun compare fairly?
qa.a: They could score both concepts on cost, rain and build time without names on them, so ownership doesn't tip the scale.

qa.q: How might the member whose concept was chosen feel about Tarun's weekend?
qa.a: That member may feel frustrated or ignored, since the better design needed help that went into fixing leaks instead.

grounding: Shows a student clinging to his own first design over a better alternative because it is his, as seen by a groupmate.

passage:
Monday. Sahil, twenty, had written the first draft of the college magazine's cover story: a long, dreamy piece about the canteen's history. Keerthana, the editor, read it and said, "Nice, but the students' strike about canteen prices is the real story. Could you rework it around that?" Sahil held the pages tight. "This one's mine. I wrote it at 2 a.m. It's good."
Wednesday. Keerthana showed him the new angle drafted by another writer, sharper and more urgent. Sahil read it and felt a small drop in his stomach. He still thought his draft was better, but he couldn't say why, except that it was his.
Friday. He sat with both pieces at the library. He asked himself: if both were written by strangers, which would I pick? The strike piece. Clearly. He walked to Keerthana's desk. "Use the strike angle. Maybe my history bit can be a side box." She grinned. "Deal."

qa.q: What was Sahil's first draft about?
qa.a: A long, dreamy piece about the canteen's history.

qa.q: Why did Sahil feel his draft was better even when he couldn't say why?
qa.a: Because he wrote it, at 2 a.m., it felt more valuable to him than any other version. His ownership made the draft seem better than it was.

qa.q: What question did Sahil ask himself on Friday, and what did it lead to?
qa.a: Which piece he'd pick if strangers had written both. The honest answer, the strike piece, led him to suggest using it with his history as a side box.

qa.q: How might Keerthana have felt when Sahil walked up to her desk on Friday?
qa.a: Keerthana was probably relieved and pleased, having waited patiently for Sahil to see it himself.

grounding: A student clings to his own first draft over a clearly better angle until he asks which he would choose if strangers wrote both.

passage: Sonali, your chacha has a confession. When I was twenty, I had an old guitar with a cracked neck. I'd bought it second-hand at sixteen and learned every song on it. In my final year I needed a laptop, and I decided to sell the guitar. I put it up for eight thousand. The music shop offered two. A friend offered two and a half. I was outraged. "Do you know how many songs I've played on this?" I kept it listed for four months. Meanwhile I wrote my project reports in the cyber café, paying by the hour. One day my roommate asked, "Saurabh, if you saw this guitar in a shop for eight thousand, would you buy it?" I laughed. Of course not. The neck was cracked. That was the day I understood it was worth eight thousand only to me. I sold it the next week.

qa.q: How much did the music shop offer for the guitar?
qa.a: The music shop offered two.

qa.q: Why was Saurabh outraged by the offers?
qa.a: The guitar held years of songs and memories for him, so it felt worth far more than its market price. Owning it made it feel special.

qa.q: What question from the roommate was the turning point?
qa.a: "If you saw this guitar in a shop for eight thousand, would you buy it?" It made Saurabh see the guitar the way a buyer would.

qa.q: How might Sonali feel hearing that Saurabh chacha kept a cracked guitar listed for four months?
qa.a: Sonali might find it funny and touching, and it could help Sonali notice when something feels precious just because it is owned. 😊

grounding: An uncle tells Sonali how at twenty he refused to sell his old guitar at the market price because it was his.

passage: Chen had written the first draft of the short film on a rainy weekend in Vancouver, and he loved every line of it. Nadia, his co-writer, came back on Monday with a second version: tighter, funnier, and the ending finally made sense. Their professor read both and circled Nadia's. "This one works." Chen felt his face go hot. "Mine has more heart," he said. "It's the original." He spent the week defending scenes that even he had yawned at, bringing back a long monologue Nadia had cut. On Friday, reading both aloud to the class, Chen heard his own draft drag. Nobody laughed where he had expected. He sat down and quietly admitted, "I think I liked it because it was mine."

qa.q: Which version did the professor circle?
qa.a: Nadia's.

qa.q: Why did Chen defend scenes he himself found dull?
qa.a: He felt protective and a bit hurt, because the draft was his original, so it felt more valuable than a better version.

qa.q: What could Chen try the next time he compares drafts?
qa.a: Read both aloud to a small group before deciding, or imagine someone else wrote both and judge which works better.

qa.q: What might that week have been like for Nadia?
qa.a: Nadia probably felt frustrated and awkward, seeing her cuts undone while trying not to hurt Chen.

grounding: A student clings to his own first draft over a better version, valuing it simply because it is his.

passage: The hostel's end-of-year sale filled the common room with mattresses, kettles and cycles. Imran had parked his old blue cycle by the door with a sign: 4,000 rupees. He had bought it three years ago for four and a half thousand. It had a squeaky chain and a bent mudguard, but it had carried him to every exam and to Ganga's birthday party in the rain. Three juniors looked at it and offered fifteen hundred. "Fifteen hundred? For this?" Imran said. "You don't know what it's been through." Ganga, the hostel secretary, checked the list: five other cycles were going for twelve to eighteen hundred. "If it were someone else's cycle, would you pay four thousand?" she asked. Imran looked at the bent mudguard and didn't answer.

qa.q: What price was on Imran's sign?
qa.a: 4,000 rupees.

qa.q: Why does Imran feel fifteen hundred is too little?
qa.a: He feels attached and a bit hurt, because the cycle carried him through three years of memories, so it seems worth far more than buyers see.

qa.q: What check does Ganga suggest, and why does it help?
qa.a: Asking whether he would pay four thousand if it were someone else's cycle, which lets him see its worth from a buyer's side.

qa.q: How do the juniors see the cycle?
qa.a: They see an old cycle with a squeaky chain and bent mudguard, worth about what the other cycles sell for.

grounding: A student prices his old cycle far above what similar cycles sell for, valuing it highly because it is his.

passage:
Dear Arohi,
I owe you an apology about the bridge model. When you suggested switching from my arch design to the truss, I argued for a whole week. I said the arch was more elegant, more "us." Honestly, it was more me. I had sketched it at 2 a.m. in first week, and I think I fell in love with it because it was mine.
Then on Thursday the load test cracked my arch at forty kilos. Your truss, which you built alone over the weekend, held sixty-five. I stood there feeling embarrassed and a bit silly.
I'd like us to go with the truss, and I'll do the write-up. Maybe I'll keep the arch sketch on my wall, as a reminder.
Harsha

qa.q: How much weight did Arohi's truss hold?
qa.a: Sixty-five kilos.

qa.q: Why did Harsha argue for the arch for a whole week?
qa.a: Harsha felt attached and proud, having sketched it at 2 a.m., so it seemed better simply because it was Harsha's own.

qa.q: What is Harsha doing to repair things with Arohi?
qa.a: Apologising honestly, choosing the truss and offering to do the write-up.

qa.q: How might Arohi feel reading this letter?
qa.a: Arohi may feel relieved and respected, since the weekend of extra work is finally acknowledged.

grounding: A student writes an apology for defending an own design over a stronger alternative, valuing it because it was theirs.

passage: Sangeeta, you asked why my old bike is still parked outside the hostel. Okay, so. It's a ten-year-old scooter, rusty, starts on the third kick if I'm lucky. My uncle gave it to me, his favourite nephew, in first year. Last month a mechanic said it's worth maybe eight thousand. I told a buyer fifteen. He laughed and left. Another offered nine. I said no. Honestly, it's mine. I learned to ride on it. I took my first road trip on it. It felt like it was worth so much more. Then I realised I haven't ridden it in six months. I take the bus. It just sits there, getting rustier. If someone offered me this scooter today for fifteen, would I buy it? No way. That's when I understood. It's only worth more because it's Manoj's.

qa.q: What did the mechanic say the scooter was worth?
qa.a: Maybe eight thousand.

qa.q: Why did Manoj ask fifteen thousand for the scooter?
qa.a: Owning it and remembering first rides made it feel far more valuable, so he felt attached and fair offers seemed too low.

qa.q: What question helped Manoj see the scooter's value more clearly?
qa.a: Asking whether he'd buy it today for fifteen thousand showed that ownership, not the market, was raising his price.

qa.q: How might the buyer who offered nine thousand see Manoj's refusal?
qa.a: The buyer might feel puzzled or annoyed, since nine was above the mechanic's estimate.

grounding: It shows a student who values his old scooter far above its market price simply because it's his.

passage:
Week one, a Monday. Akash had written the first draft of the script for the college short-film competition. He loved it: a long, slow story about a village postman. His teammate Suraj read it and said, "It's beautiful, but it's twenty minutes. The limit is ten. What if we do my idea about the hostel water tank? It's funny and short."

Week two, a Thursday. Akash had cut his script to fifteen minutes. "It's still too long," Suraj said. Akash refused to switch. "My draft is better. It has heart." He felt it was his, and that made it precious.

Week four, a Friday. The deadline came. Their film was fourteen minutes, and it was disqualified for going over the limit. Suraj's water-tank idea, which another team had made with a similar plot, won second prize. Akash sat in the auditorium, stung, holding his draft.

qa.q: How long was Akash's first draft?
qa.a: Twenty minutes.

qa.q: Why did Akash refuse to switch to Suraj's idea?
qa.a: His own draft felt precious because it was his, so he valued it above a better-fitting idea, and later felt stung.

qa.q: What could Akash have asked himself in week two?
qa.a: He could have asked whether he'd choose his draft over Suraj's if neither were his, judging both by the ten-minute rule.

qa.q: How might Suraj feel about the disqualification?
qa.a: Suraj likely feels frustrated and disappointed, since his idea fit the rules and another team won with something similar.

grounding: It shows a student who refuses to drop his first draft because it's his, valuing it above a better alternative, over several weeks.

passage: Akash, you're stuck on your thesis chapter? Let me tell you what I did in final year. I was a young man of twenty-one, writing a project on rainwater harvesting in Chennai. My first draft had a long history section I loved. Three pages about old temple tanks. My guide said, "Ojas, this doesn't fit. Cut it and add your field data." I couldn't. It was my writing, my discovery. I defended it for weeks. My friend offered a better structure. I said no, because the old one felt like mine. In the end, I got a lower mark because the data section was thin. Later I asked myself: if someone else had written those three pages, would I keep them? No. I kept them only because they were mine.

qa.q: What was the history section in Ojas's draft about?
qa.a: Old temple tanks.

qa.q: Why did young Ojas refuse to cut the history section?
qa.a: The section felt precious because it was his own writing and discovery, so he valued it above a better structure.

qa.q: At what point in the story could Ojas have chosen differently?
qa.a: When the guide said to cut it and add field data, asking whether he'd keep those pages if someone else wrote them could have helped him let go.

qa.q: How might Ojas's guide have felt about the thin data section?
qa.a: The guide may have felt disappointed, having warned him that the history section didn't fit.

grounding: It shows an elder recalling how, as a student, he refused to drop a part of his draft because it was his, valuing it above a better alternative.

passage:
Karthik had two days to empty his hostel room, and his old bicycle stood by the door, rusty chain, flat back tyre.

"Pranav, I'll sell it for four thousand."

Pranav laughed. "Bro, nobody will give more than one thousand for that. The shop outside charges six thousand for a new one."

"It's special. I rode it everywhere for three years."

Three first-years came to look. One offered eight hundred. Another offered a thousand. Karthik refused both. "They don't get what it's worth."

By the last evening, nobody had bought it. The bike stood there, and Karthik couldn't take it on the train.

"Would you pay four thousand for it?" Pranav asked.

Karthik looked at the rust. "No," he said quietly. "Not a chance."

He sold it to the first-year for a thousand, and felt oddly sad handing over the key.

qa.q: How much did Karthik first ask for the bicycle?
qa.a: I'll sell it for four thousand.

qa.q: Why did Karthik refuse the first-years' offers?
qa.a: Karthik felt attached and sad about the bike after three years of riding it, so it seemed worth far more than its market value.

qa.q: What question from Pranav helped Karthik, and why?
qa.a: Pranav asked whether Karthik would pay four thousand for the bike himself, which showed the gap between owner and buyer value.

qa.q: How might the first-years have seen Karthik's price?
qa.a: The first-years probably found it far too high for a rusty bike with a flat tyre.

grounding: Under a deadline to leave the hostel, a student prices his old bike far above what buyers will pay because it is his.

passage:
For the final-year project, Dhruv had written a first draft proposal: a water-quality sensor for the college lake. He'd spent a week on it. He loved it.

In the group meeting, his teammate Omkar shared a different idea: a sensor for measuring air quality in classrooms, with a clear plan, a smaller budget, and a professor already interested.

Dhruv felt his chest tighten. "Mine's more original."

"It needs equipment we don't have," Omkar said gently. "And no professor has agreed to guide it."

"We can work it out."

The other two teammates looked at each other.

That night, Dhruv read both proposals side by side. If someone else had written his, and he'd written Omkar's, which would he pick?

Omkar's. Easily.

It stung. His draft was his. But the next morning, he sent the group a message: "Let's go with Omkar's. I'll bring my lake ideas as a side test."

qa.q: What was Dhruv's first draft proposal about?
qa.a: A water-quality sensor for the college lake.

qa.q: Why did Dhruv feel his chest tighten when Omkar shared his idea?
qa.a: Dhruv felt defensive because his own draft felt precious simply because he wrote it and loved it.

qa.q: What did Dhruv do that helped him judge fairly?
qa.a: Dhruv imagined the proposals had swapped authors and asked which he'd pick, which showed Omkar's was better.

qa.q: How might Omkar feel when Dhruv agrees to Omkar's idea?
qa.a: Omkar might feel relieved and grateful, and appreciate Dhruv bringing the lake ideas as a side test.

grounding: A student clings to his own first-draft proposal over a better alternative because it is his, until he swaps authors in his mind.

passage:
"Omkar, we need to decide the app idea today."

"I already told you, Rajni. My study timer app."

"Yours has no users in testing. Mine, the hostel laundry tracker, had fifty sign-ups in a day."

"Mine's more polished. I've been working on it since first year."

"That's kind of the problem. You're attached."

"I'm not attached. It's just better."

"Okay. Pretend I built the timer and you built the laundry tracker. Which would you choose?"

"...That's not fair."

"Just answer."

Omkar stared at the screen. "The laundry one. It has users."

"So?"

"So it's hard to let go of mine because it's mine."

"You can keep working on it. Just not for this competition."

Omkar sighed. "Fine. Laundry. But I'm keeping the timer's logo."

qa.q: How many sign-ups did the laundry tracker get in a day?
qa.a: Fifty sign-ups in a day.

qa.q: Why did Omkar insist the study timer was better?
qa.a: Omkar felt attached to the timer after working on it since first year, so owning it made it seem better than it was.

qa.q: What did Rajni ask that helped Omkar decide?
qa.a: Rajni asked Omkar to imagine the ideas had swapped owners, which showed the laundry tracker was stronger.

qa.q: How does Rajni seem to feel during the argument?
qa.a: Rajni seems patient but firm, wanting a fair decision without dismissing Omkar's work.

grounding: A student holds on to an app idea over a better one simply because it is theirs, until asked to imagine swapping owners.

passage: The monsoon was ending when I moved out of the hostel, and I had to decide about my cycle. It was a heavy black thing with a rusted bell, bought secondhand in first year. I'd fixed the chain myself twice. Aadhya from the next wing wanted it for her brother. "The seniors' board says old cycles go for about eighteen hundred," she said. "I'll give two thousand." I said five thousand. She looked at me as if I'd lost my mind. Honestly, I felt insulted. That cycle had carried me through every exam week. In the end nobody paid five thousand, and I couldn't take it on the train, so it's still chained outside the hostel, rusting in the last rains. Aadhya's brother bought a different one. I still laugh at myself sometimes: Pranav the great dealer, holding out for a price only Pranav believed in.

qa.q: How much did Aadhya offer for the cycle?
qa.a: Aadhya offered two thousand.

qa.q: Why did Pranav feel insulted by Aadhya's offer?
qa.a: The cycle held memories of fixing the chain and getting through exam weeks, so to Pranav it felt worth far more than its price, and a fair offer felt like a slight.

qa.q: What check could Pranav have used before naming a price?
qa.a: Pranav could have asked whether anyone, Pranav included, would pay five thousand for that cycle today, and compared it with the prices on the seniors' board.

qa.q: How did Aadhya likely react to the price of five thousand?
qa.a: Aadhya was probably baffled and put off, since the offer was already above the usual price, so Aadhya's brother bought a different cycle.

grounding: Shows a student refusing to sell an old cycle because it is theirs, valuing it well above what any buyer would pay.
